1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Shape stationarity hypothesis.}
5	Upper-tail features remain near-stationary because the softmax architecture and sampling hyperparameters that determine distributional shape are fixed across depths; recursive generation shifts context toward high-probability regions (reducing entropy mean) without altering the generation mechanism itself.
6	This predicts stationarity until the model reaches its fixed-point distribution, a regime not observed at chain length $\leq$4.
7	Sampling ablation supports this: depth signal is robust at $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ (${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation) but breaks down at $t = 1.0$ ($-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where sampling noise dominates distributional shape.
8	
9	\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}
10	Continuation chains yield the strongest signal (F1\,=\,0.781 vs.\ 0.730 for elaboration), with cross-type transfer at 0.753 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
11	Semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift, consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}.
12	
13	\paragraph{Practical applicability.}
14	At the document level, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 (37\% misclassification) is insufficient for automated filtering but suitable for flagging; at the corpus level, error scales as $O(1/\sqrt{n})$, making aggregate depth composition estimates reliable.
15	A detailed error analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}) confirms that errors concentrate in shallow gen-2+ samples where distributional drift is insufficient, consistent with DDR predictions.
16	
17	\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
18	Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs; our inference-chain drift occurs without parameter updates, representing an early, reversible stage of the same narrowing.
19	Topic drift accounts for $<$9\% of feature variance ($R^2 = 0.082$), confirming it mediates rather than confounds depth signal.
20	
21	\paragraph{Scope boundaries.}
22	Three classes represent the practical granularity ceiling: 5-class LOGO F1 drops to $\approx$0.50, with gen-2/gen-3 inseparable (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}); QLoRA fine-tuning recovers 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming signal beyond summary statistics.

24	Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.764 base), justifying our restriction to base models.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text (estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}), and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself (how distributional features evolve across generation depths) remains underexplored.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using eight base (pretrained) models from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral) spanning multiple scales.
We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds (output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores span a wide performance range (binary F1 from 0.53 to 0.68; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable for depth discrimination.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while upper-tail features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
We hypothesize that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution with partial shape preservation; under this account, the softmax ceiling constrains upper-tail behavior regardless of input content, while variance shows moderate drift.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves F1\,=\,0.764 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and binary F1\,=\,0.694 under the strict leave-one-generator-out protocol (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+).
However, the strength of this signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains exhibit stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting chains (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

We additionally report a negative finding: despite the effectiveness of quality-based data curation for pretraining \cite{fineweb,dolma}, depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 vs.\ 2.387).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation depths.
        \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across eight base-model generators spanning five model families: a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains and binary F1\,=\,0.694 under strict unseen-generator evaluation, with a single lightweight reference model, significantly outperforming individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, and baseline comparisons.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses mechanistic hypotheses and scope boundaries.
